content: The relationship between dietary antioxidants and conditions such as asthma or exercise-induced bronchoconstriction (EIB) remains incompletely understood. Vitamin C and vitamin E are natural antioxidants primarily found in fruits and vegetables. Insufficient intake of vitamin E has been linked to airway inflammation. It has been hypothesized that the combined use of these two antioxidants may provide greater benefits than using either one alone for individuals with asthma or EIB. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effects of vitamin C and E supplementation compared to placebo (or no supplementation) on asthma exacerbations and health-related quality of life (HRQL) in both adults and children with chronic asthma. Additionally, the review aimed to explore the potential effects of these vitamins on EIB in individuals with asthma and in those without asthma who experience symptoms only during exercise. To identify relevant studies, researchers searched the Cochrane Airways Review Group Specialised Register and trial registry websites in September 2013. The review included randomized controlled trials involving adults and children diagnosed with asthma. Separate consideration was given to trials involving participants with EIB (or exercise-induced asthma). Only trials comparing vitamin C and E supplementation to placebo were included, and all studies ensured that asthma management strategies were similar between treatment and control groups. Short-term use of these vitamins during exacerbations or for cold symptoms in individuals with asthma was excluded from the review. Two independent reviewers screened the titles, abstracts, and full-text reports of potential studies for inclusion. Standard Cochrane Collaboration methods were used for data collection and analysis. The review included five studies with a total of 214 participants. Four studies (206 participants) investigated the effects of vitamin C and E supplementation versus placebo in individuals with asthma. Of these, only one study (160 children) involved a pediatric population, while the remaining three studies included a total of just 46 adults. One additional study examined the effects of these vitamins on EIB, involving only eight participants. The randomization process in these trials was unclear, leading to a downgrade in the quality of the evidence. Four studies were double-blind, while one was single-blind. None of the included studies provided data on the two primary outcomes of interest: asthma exacerbations and HRQL. Lung function data from the studies were inconclusive. The only studies suggesting any potential effects were the pediatric study, particularly in children with moderate to severe asthma, and the small study on EIB. However, the evidence from these studies was judged to be of moderate to low quality. Only one study reported data on asthma symptoms and adverse events, finding no significant effect of the intervention on symptoms. One participant in the treatment group dropped out due to cystitis. The authors concluded that it is not possible to draw definitive conclusions regarding the effects of vitamin C and E supplementation compared to placebo in the management of asthma or EIB. Only one study specifically addressed EIB, and most participants in the included studies were part of trials designed to assess the impact of vitamin supplementation on atmospheric pollutants, such as ozone. There is a lack of evidence on the effects of vitamin C and E supplementation on key outcomes such as HRQL and exacerbations, which were not addressed by any of the included studies. HRQL scores and exacerbation frequency are considered better indicators of asthma severity, its impact on daily life, and treatment response compared to lung function tests alone. These endpoints are well-recognized in high-quality asthma management studies. However, clinical trials investigating the role of vitamins C and E in asthma management using these important endpoints are unavailable. As a result, the evidence is insufficient to support strong conclusions about the role of vitamin C and E supplementation in asthma or exercise-induced breathlessness.
